title.en: The Guilty Hunters: The Face in the Water and the Bitten Thumb
title.zh: 有罪的獵人：水中之臉與被咬的拇指

region.en: Neighboring hunting camps of two clans by a stream

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The guilty hunters'

summary.en: Two families camp side by side; one has fine luck, the other none. A mother sees in the stream the reflection of a handsome man with painted cheeks hidden in the branches - a man from the adjoining camp - and reads it as an evil omen. The husband sends her and the child into a hollow log and meets the robbers alone: 'You have bitten me.' She hides in a hemlock over the murderers' camp, hears one say his thumb is painful - 'say a beaver bit you' - and at the general council convicts them: the chief says gravely, 'Go, do your duty,' and the warriors soon put to death the wicked hunters.
summary.zh: 兩族比鄰紮營，一家獵運亨通，一家一無所獲。一位母親在溪水中窺見藏在枝頭、面頰敷彩的俊美男子——正是鄰營之人——她視之為凶兆。丈夫送妻兒藏入空心圓木，隻身赴險：「你咬了我。」她藏身於兇手營上的鐵杉，聽見有人說拇指疼痛——「就說是河狸咬的」——並在大議會上指證兇徒。酋長沉聲道：「去吧，盡你們的職責。」戰士們隨即誅殺了這些惡獵人。

passages.text: In one of its hunting excursions two families of different clans happened to pitch their camps quite near each other. One, in which there was an infant, had very fine luck and the other poor luck. While the father of the child was out hunting, the mother went to a neighboring stream to get some water, but before she dipped her vessel she looked into the water and saw, peering up through the sparkling stream, a very handsome young man with painted cheeks. What the woman had seen was but the reflection of some one hidden in the branches overhanging the stream, and she recognized the face as that of a man from the adjoining camp. They rightly judged that this was an evil omen.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: When night came the husband said to his wife, 'You and the child must be saved. Go; I shall meet misfortune alone.' She started with the child through the forest until she came to a hollow log, into which she crept; soon she heard a great noise in the camp, and a voice saying, 'You have bitten me.' Torches came searching for her and the child, pushing their sticks into the log, and saying, 'She must be somewhere near here; any way, she cannot live long.' She traveled parallel to the trail and climbed a large hemlock in a clearing, where during the night she heard one of the laden hunters say, 'My thumb is painful; what shall I say bit me?' and the answer: 'Say a beaver bit you.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Reaching home at twilight, she related what had happened, and the head chief called a general council. None but the hunters were absent, and they came after repeated and persistent requests. 'Now, relate to us all the things that have happened to you,' said the head chief, 'and tell why you have returned without the other party.' They refused to tell anything. When she had finished her narrative she told that one of them had his thumb bitten - by her husband in defending himself against these robbers, who took from her murdered husband the skins and the meats. Hereupon the head chief gravely said to the waiting and impatient warriors, 'Go, do your duty'; and they, with their war-clubs and tomahawks, soon put to death the wicked hunters.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Mrs. Logan's Story: The Skeleton's Island and the Pit Under the Bed
title.zh: 羅根夫人所述：骷髏之島與床下之坑

region.en: Swan-propelled island in a great lake, and a cranberry swamp beyond
region.zh: 天鵝舟所達的湖心島，以及更遠的蔓越莓沼澤

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Mrs. Logan's story'

summary.en: A boy invited to shoot and swim with a stranger is stripped and abandoned on an island. A skeleton near him - mice driven out by pipe smoke - coaches him through the visits of the three-dog man: track the island, jump in and out of the water, sleep in a hollow tree, and lie hidden in a sand pit at the landing until the abductor comes to drink his blood - then steal the swan canoe, 'Come, swans, let's go home,' and never look back. In a rock cave he finds his own clothes; sent east, he rescues the sister the man carried off, hides her brother under her bed-planks, kills the water-drinking abductor with a thrown stone, turns his dogs into wolves, and raises the dead of the skeleton's island to build a long house with six fire-places.
summary.zh: 男孩應陌生人邀約賽射、比泳，被剝衣棄於島上。身旁的骷髏（菸煙驅走滿身鼠群）指導他應付三犬男子：踏遍全島、屢次跳入又躍出水中、夜宿空心樹、藏身沙坑待其登岸吸血——再竊天鵝舟唱「天鵝們，我們回家吧」，永不回頭。岩洞中他尋回己衣；被遣往東方，他救回多年前被擄的姐姐，藏身其床板下的坑中，以擲石誅殺飲水脹身的擄人者，令其犬化為狼，並喚醒骷髏島上的死者，共建六灶長屋。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Cannibalism is attributed to the villain and reported at story distance.

passages.text: An old man and his little nephew once lived in a dark woods. The boy, tired of playing in one place, went to a large lake, where a man came up and said, 'Let us play together at shooting arrows... Let us go to the island, where you will see many pretty birds.' On either side of the canoe were three swans which propelled it. As soon as they were seated the man began singing, and very soon they arrived at the island; then the man took off all the boy's clothes and, jumping into his canoe, said, 'Come, swans, let us go home.' It began to grow dark, and the boy was greatly frightened when he heard a voice say, 'Hist! keep still' - a skeleton on the ground near him beckoned: 'Poor boy, it was the same thing with me, but I will help you if you will do something for me.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The skeleton told him to dig on the west side of a tree near by for a tobacco-pouch, a pipe, and a flint, fill and light the pipe and put it in its mouth; then, as the skeleton smoked, the boy saw that its body was full of mice, which went away because of the smoke. 'A man with three dogs is coming to the island that night to kill me... you must run all over the island and jump into the water and out again many times, so that the man will lose the trail; then get into a hollow tree near by, and stay all night.' The dogs ran all over the island, found nothing, and the man killed one of his dogs and ate him all up. 'The man who brought you here will come to-night to drink your blood; dig a long pit at the shore... and when he comes ashore, get into the canoe and say, Come, swans, let's go home - and if the man calls for you to come back you must not turn around or look at him.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The boy jumped into the canoe, singing as the man had done; the man cried, 'Come back! Oh do come back!' but the boy did not look around. The swans went up into a large rock to a door, and in the cave he found his own clothes and many others, a fire and food all prepared. Returning to the island he found the man killed and nearly eaten up. 'Now you must go and get your sister whom this man carried off many years ago... you will come to some very high rocks where she goes for water.' A bad man kept her there; while he was away at the swamp where women and children were picking cranberries, the sister dug a pit under her bed-planks and covered her brother in it, then cooked a little boy for the man's supper. The dogs barked; 'You surely have visitors,' he said. 'Kill me if you like, but I have none,' she denied - and the saucy answers told him she had seen some one.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: In the morning she called her brother, they jumped into the canoe and went off, but the man ran and threw a hook which caught the canoe; the boy broke it with a stone from the bottom. Then the enraged man laid himself down upon the shore and drank the water from the lake, causing the boat to return very fast, until he grew very big with so much water in him; the boy threw a stone and hit the man so it killed him, and the water ran back into the lake. The boy said to the two dogs, 'You bad dogs... You must go into the woods and be wolves,' and they became wolves. At the island the skeleton said, 'Gather up all the bones you see and put them in a pile; then push the largest tree you see and say, All dead folks arise - and they will all arise.' All the dead arose, some having but one arm, some with but one leg, but all had their bows and arrows; the boy and his sister brought them home, and they built a long house with six fire-places, where they lived peacefully many years.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Hunter and His Dead Wife: The Wooden Doll Returned
title.zh: 獵人與亡妻：歸來的木偶

region.en: Forest cabin far from the rest of the tribe

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The hunter and his dead wife'

summary.en: After his wife dies, a lonely hunter dresses a wooden doll in her clothes and sets it by the fire-place, brushing the fallen ashes from its face. Then fire and wood appear by the door, meat cooks in the kettle - and one early return he finds his wife sitting in the chair, the doll gone. 'The Great Spirit felt sorry for you, so he let me come back to see you, but you must not touch me till we have seen all of our people; if you do, you will kill me.' Within a day's journey of the camp his desire overcomes him; he clasps her - and holds the wooden doll. The tracks in the snow end like a doll's feet, and the man was ever after very unhappy.
summary.zh: 妻死之後，孤獨的獵人以她的衣物裝扮一具木偶置於灶前，日日拂去落於面上的灰燼。隨後門前有火有柴，釜中有肉——一日早歸，他見亡妻端坐椅上，木偶不見。她說：「大神憐你，讓我回來看你；但在見過所有族人之前不可碰我，否則我會死。」距營地一日路程處，他的渴望戰勝了戒律；他擁她入懷——抱著的卻是木偶。雪中的足跡末端恰似偶足。此後他鬱鬱終老。

passages.text: The man felt very badly and buried her in the cabin. He was very lonesome; and after a day or two he made a wooden doll about her size and dressed it in the clothes she used to wear. Then he put it down in front of the fire-place and felt better. Then he went hunting; and when he came back he would go up to the doll and brush the ashes off from the face, for as the wood fell down the ashes would rattle onto the face. He had to do his cooking, mending, and making fire, for now there was no one to help him; and so a year passed away.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: One day when he came home from hunting there was a fire and wood by the door. The next night there was wood and fire and a piece of meat all cooked in the kettle. He looked all over to see who had done this, but could find no one. The next time he went hunting he did not go far and went back quite early, and when he came in sight of the cabin he saw a woman going into the house with wood on her shoulders; he opened the door quickly, and there was his wife sitting in a chair and the wooden doll was gone.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Then she spoke to him, saying, 'The Great Spirit felt sorry for you, so he let me come back to see you, but you must not touch me till we have seen all of our people; if you do, you will kill me.' So they lived along for some time... When they were within a day's journey of the camp it began to snow, and as they were very weary they lighted fire and partook of food and spread their skins to sleep; but the desire of the man to once more clasp his wife in his arms was too great, and he went up to her and put out his hands; but she motioned him away and said, 'We have seen no one yet.' He would not listen to her, and he caught her in his arms, and, behold, he was holding the wooden doll! His sorrow was very great. Some doubted, and they went back with him and found the doll; they also saw the track of the two people in the snow, and the track just like the foot of the doll. The man was ever after very unhappy.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: A Sure Revenge: Ga-geh-djo-wa Among the Illinois
title.zh: 必償之仇：伊利諾人中的加格卓瓦

region.en: Seneca settlement on Lake Erie and the Illinois country (traditional)
region.zh: 伊利湖畔的塞內卡聚落與伊利諾之地（傳統）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'A sure revenge'

summary.en: The Illinois surprise a Seneca settlement and carry off a woman and a boy, who sings his vow of revenge in his own tongue while they think he joins their triumph. The woman is slain after charging him: 'Avenge my blood! Promise me you will never cease to be a Seneca.' Tortured - barefooted on coals, blisters pierced and filled with flint, a race over thorn-briers, the stake, and three drownings - he survives, is adopted as Ga-geh-djo-wa, and fifteen years later leads the Illinois war party against his own people, guides them into an ambush of five hundred Senecas, and stumbles as the signal: three hundred scalps avenge the treachery of the Illinois.
summary.zh: 伊利諾人偷襲伊利湖畔的塞內卡聚落，擄走一名婦人與男孩。男孩以本族語言反覆唱著復仇之誓，敵人以為他同慶。婦人臨刑囑咐：「為我復仇！答應我永不背棄塞內卡。」他歷盡酷刑——赤足踏炭、水泡刺破填入燧石、荊棘叢中賽跑、火刑柱、三次溺水——竟得存活，被收養為加格卓瓦。十五年後他率伊利諾戰隊攻擊族人，將其引入五百塞內卡戰士的埋伏，以跌倒為號——三百枚髮皮為伊利諾人的背信償命。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Captivity-torture narrative of record; grim but historical register.

passages.text: One eventful winter their enemies, the Illinois, came in great numbers upon the peaceful settlement, surprised the people in their homes, and, in spite of a stout resistance, killed a large number of them and took a middle-aged woman and a boy captive. Around a roaring fire the warriors gloated over the bloody deed, and bid the boy join them in their songs of triumph. The lad pretended that he could not sing their language, but said that he would sing their song in his tongue, knowing that they could not comprehend a word of it. While they shouted out their jubilant delight he repeated, again and again, 'I shall never forget what you have done to my people... If I am spared you will all lose your scalps.' The Illinois warriors understood not a word; they thought he was joining in their triumph.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After they had marched three days the woman became exhausted, and she was too faint to be dragged further. She meanwhile spoke to the Seneca boy in earnest tones: 'Avenge my blood!... and when you return to your own people tell them how the cruel Illinois took my life. Promise me you will never cease to be a Seneca.' As he finished promising all she asked, she was slain and left dead on the ground. At the Illinois settlement the chiefs decided that there was stuff in him, and they would therefore torture him: they held him barefooted on the coals until his feet were one mass of blisters, pierced the blisters with a needle made of fish bone and filled them up with sharp flint stones. 'Now run a race - run twenty rods.' In his dream he had been told that if he could reach the Long House and find a seat on the wild-cat skin, they would vote him worthy of his life. Singing what they thought their war song, he forgot his agony, bounded forward and flew so swiftly that those ready to hit him with thorn-brier branches could not touch him; he rushed into the crowded Long House and managed to seat himself upon the tail of the wild-cat skin.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: The majority finally decided that he must die, and in three days should be burned at the stake. When the day arrived they bound the lad to a stake amid a large fire of pine knots, when an old warrior suddenly approached from the forest: 'His eye is bright. I will take him. I will make a warrior of him... and if he survives I will adopt him into the tribe.' He cut the thongs and led him away to a spring: 'Drink!' And as the lad stooped, he pressed him down under the water until he was well nigh strangled; three times he subjected him to this barbarity; then as he was still alive he took him to his wigwam and dressed his feet - and no one guessed that revenge was in his heart.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: He had been fifteen years among them when he heard them speak of an expedition against the Senecas. He begged to join, and they elected him chief of the expedition. At the council held that night Ga-geh-djo-wa proposed to go himself with another warrior; when they had gone five or six miles the wily chief said, 'Let us separate... You go over the hills; I will go through the valley.' He found a family he knew: 'The treacherous Illinois are upon you. Warn all the tribe of Senecas: bid them come early and hide along the range above the valley. I will be there with a heron's plume on my crest, and when I stumble it is the signal for the Senecas to attack.' Returning, he reported that he had seen nothing; then he offered to track the Senecas to their hiding-place. Little they dreamed that already five hundred Senecas awaited them in the valley. As they entered it, he, pretending to miss his footing, fell: instantly the war-cry sounded, the Senecas rushed from their ambush, and the slaughter was great. Three hundred scalps revenged the treachery of the Illinois, and Ga-geh-djo-wa lived many years, the most esteemed warrior and chief of the Senecas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

region.zh: 易洛魁各鎮之間的村道

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Traveler's jokes'

summary.en: Tired of an uneventful journey, a traveler abuses the runners' cry 'Goh-weh, goh-weh' to gather crowds, then invents news: at the last village they danced for joy and kissed him - so the crowd, not wishing to be outdone, sings and kisses him too; at the next town some wept and quarreled, so his audience does the same. Camping with a boastful stranger he asks what log he pillows on - hickory, elm? 'No, it is everlasting sleep' - and in the morning rubs pitchy resin over the sleeper's eyes and leaves, laughing.
summary.zh: 旅途無聊的旅人濫用信使的呼聲「果威，果威」召聚人群，編造新聞：上個村子的人歡舞親吻他——聽者不甘落後，也唱歌親吻；下一鎮則有人哭泣鬥毆——聽者如法炮製。夜宿時他問自誇機智的同伴枕的是什麼木——胡桃？榆木？「不，是長眠之木」；清晨他在睡者眼上抹滿松脂，笑著離去。

passages.text: An old Indian custom is for runners, or those carrying important news, to announce the fact and gather the people together by crying, in singing tones, 'Goh-weh, goh-weh.' This the traveler began doing, and when the crowd called upon him to stop and tell his news, he began, 'As I came through the last village the people were so delighted with my news that they all danced for joy, and shouted and kissed me.' This he told so earnestly and sincerely that the people, not wishing to be outdone by any other tribe, also began singing and kissing him and making merry; and while the excitement was at its height, pleased with his success, the facetious traveler escaped and continued his journeyings.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: Arrived at the next village he again began calling, 'Goh-weh, goh-weh'; and the people and chiefs gathered around him, crying, 'Let us hear.' And he answered, 'As I passed through the last town some people wept at my news, others began quarreling, kicking, and fighting.' Immediately his contagious news produced its effect, and in the confusion he again escaped, saying to himself, 'What fools people are.' That night, as he was preparing to camp out, a man passed who inquired the distance to the next village; but the traveler said, 'You cannot reach it to-night. Let us camp together.' As the new-comer was boasting of his superior cunning, the traveler inquired, 'What log is that you now use for a pillow?' and he guessed hickory, elm. But the traveler said, 'No, it is everlasting sleep.' In the morning the traveler took some pitchy resin and rubbed over the eyes of his sleeping comrade and left, laughing at the probable chagrin the man would feel when attempting to open his eyes.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: Kingfisher and His Nephew: The Sticks in the Nose and the Stolen Wings
title.zh: 翠鳥與姪兒：鼻中之枝與被竊的翅膀

region.en: River log and a lovely island, Seneca Reservation (Zachariah Jamieson informant)
region.zh: 河上圓木與可愛的島嶼，塞內卡保留地（扎卡里亞詹姆森講述）

texts.period: Told by Zachariah Jamieson, from Chief Warrior (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'Kingfisher and his nephew'

summary.en: Forbidden to fish west, the nephew spies his uncle To-be-se-ne sticking two sharp sticks up his nose and plunging deep for fish; trying it himself he nearly dies of the ache. Later he joins boys with wings who invite him to swim for distance - and fly away with his clothes and wings, calling 'Uncle, here is game for you to-night.' Hiding tree to tree from the many-faced man's dogs all night, he ambushes the winged boys next morning, seizes every pair, and flies home crying, 'Uncle, now there is plenty of game for you' - 'You had no mercy on me; I only treat you the same.'
summary.zh: 姪兒被禁向西捕魚，卻偷看叔父托貝塞內將兩根尖枝插入鼻孔潛水抓魚；自己一試幾乎痛死。其後他遇上有翼的少年們邀他比賽潛泳——他們卻連衣物帶翅膀全部帶走，喊著「叔叔，今晚有你想要的獵物」飛走。他藏於一樹又一樹，躲過有雙面男人的獵犬整夜；翌晨伏擊有翼少年們，奪走全部翅膀，飛回家中喊道：「叔叔，現在有很多獵物了」——「你們對我沒有憐憫，我也同樣對待你們。」

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. The uncle is the kingfisher-bird in human form.

passages.text: The old man said to his nephew, 'When you are a man, remember in hunting never to go west; always go to the east.' The young man reflected: 'Why should this be so? My uncle To-be-se-ne always goes west, and brings home plenty of fish.' He made up his mind at last that he would go. As he passed the marsh land near the river he saw his uncle take from his pocket two sharp sticks and put them in his nose, and then plunge into deep water and come up with a nice fish. Presently the uncle came back bringing some nice fish, but he never guessed that the nephew had seen him. The young man now felt certain that he could fish as well as his uncle; one day he stuck the two sticks into his nose and plunged in - then the sticks went deep into his nose and made it ache dreadfully, and he felt very sick. 'You have done very wrong,' said the uncle; but he took the pincers and drew out the sticks.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After a while, however, he started west again. He heard boys laughing, joined them, and they invited him to swim. 'It is time to go home; you go, too.' Then he saw that they had wings, and they gave him a pair: 'There is an island where all is lovely... come.' They started up in the air, far away above the trees. 'Let us see which can go down and come up the farthest'; and while he was in the water the rest put on their wings and, taking his also, flew up in the air. He plead in vain for them to wait; but they called, as though speaking to some one else, 'Uncle, here is game for you to-night.' He perceived tracks of dogs which had clawed the different trees; to confuse them in their scent he climbed each tree a little way until he reached the last tree on the island. The man had a horrid-looking face, both behind and before; the dogs traced him tree by tree all night long, until the old man said, very angrily, 'There is no game here; my nephews have deceived me.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: After sunrise the poor fellow came down from the tree, saying, 'If those young fellows return I will watch them and contrive to get their wings from them.' He soon heard their voices, saying, 'Now we will have a good time... Let us all dive together.' Then he rushed out, and, taking all the wings, he put on one pair, and flew away, calling out, 'Uncle, now there is plenty of game for you'; and when they entreated him he replied, 'You had no mercy on me; I only treat you the same.' Then he flew on until he came to his old home, where he found his old uncle, to whom he recounted the whole story; and after that time he remained peacefully at home with his good uncle. 'So many times my old grandfather, chief Warrior, told me that story,' said Zachariah Jamieson.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The Wild-Cat and the White Rabbit: The Song That Closed the Circle

region.en: Deep woods near the Seneca Reservation (Zachariah Jamieson informant)
region.zh: 塞內卡保留地附近的深林（扎卡里亞詹姆森講述）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. V: 'The wild-cat and the white rabbit'

summary.en: Lonely for companionship, the wild-cat sings a plaintive ditty whose meaning is 'When you are frightened, sweet rabbit, you run in a circle.' The white rabbit hears the dangerous voice and scuds away - but, hearing the song again and again, ever nearer, he follows his instinct and runs in a circle, which brings him each time closer to his enemy, until, circling ever nearer, he falls a victim to the wild-cat.
summary.zh: 渴望同伴的野貓唱出一支哀歌，其意為：「受驚的甜兔兒啊，你會繞圈而逃。」白兔聽出那危險的嗓音便狂奔而逃——但歌聲一次次更近，牠只能順從天性繞圈而跑，每次都更接近敵人；圈愈縮愈小，白兔終成野貓的獵物。

passages.text: The wild cat, roaming disconsolately in the woods, experienced the sense of utter loneliness which calls for companionship. A friend he must have or die. Cats there were none within speaking distance, but rabbits it might be possible to entice. He commenced a plaintive ditty: 'He gah yah neh, He gah yah! He gah yah, Di ho ni shu gua da-se, He yah gah.' His meaning was simple as his song: 'When you are frightened, sweet rabbit, you run in a circle.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

passages.text: A short distance off lay a white rabbit in his lair; hearing the melodious ditty he pricked up his ears. 'Heigho!' exclaimed he, 'that dangerous fellow, the wild-cat, is around; I hear his voice; I must scud'; and away he ran, turning from the direction in which the voice came. He had gone but a short distance when he stopped, turned back his ears and listened - there was the song again, and again, nearer each time. Unfortunate rabbit! he could but follow his instinct and run in a circle which brought him each time nearer his enemy. Still the song went on, until, circling ever nearer, white rabbit fell a victim to the wild-cat.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. V; public domain.

title.en: The New-Year Festival of the Onondagas: Confession, White Dog, and the Scaring of Witches
title.zh: 奧農達加新年祭：懺悔、白犬與驅巫

texts.period: Observed by Smith c. 1878-1881; Handsome Lake's teaching introduced 'nearly a century ago' (1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. VI: 'New-Year festival'

summary.en: At the first new moon of the new year the chiefs assemble a 'holy meeting': four days of speeches introducing the sayings of Handsome Lake, chiefs' and warriors' confession over the wampum ('I have been drunk; I have sinned'), the feather dance, the clan games of Bear-Deer-Eel-Hawk against Wolf-Beaver-Snipe-Turtle, three days of religious gambling - then the scaring of witches, costumed messenger-spirits stirring the ashes, and the roasting of a spotless white dog strangled by five young men of spotless reputation, combed with teasels, decorated with wampum and tobacco, and thrown into the fire while the warriors shoot up at the sun. The festival closes after three weeks with the medicine men chasing diseases from house to house and throwing ashes on the assembled people.
summary.zh: 新年首個新月，酋長們舉行「聖會」：四日講述漢森湖之言，酋長與戰士執貝珠懺悔（「我飲過酒；我犯過罪」），行羽舞，熊鹿鰻鷹對狼狸鷸龜的氏族競賽，三日宗教性賭戲——繼而「驅巫」，化身精靈的使者攪動灰燼；並由五名名聲無瑕的青年絞殺一隻純潔無疵的白犬，以 teasel 梳毛、飾以貝珠與菸草，在戰士們向日射箭之際投入火中。三週後，醫者逐屋驅病、向群眾揚灰，祭典方告終。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. An outside observer's 1880s account of the Midwinter rites; presented as ethnographic description, not ritual instruction. The white-dog sacrifice is described historically.

passages.text: At the first new moon of the new year the chiefs assemble and call what they term a 'holy meeting': a bench is placed in the center of the circle of chiefs, upon which are placed their strings of Indian wampum. One then rises and makes a long speech, in which he introduces the sayings, maxims, and teachings of Handsome Lake, who, nearly a century ago, introduced a new form into the Seneca religion. Speeches of this kind occupy four days. On the fifth day the principal chiefs, taking hold of the wampum, say: 'I put all my words in this wampum'; 'I have been drunk'; or, 'I have sinned.' On the sixth day the warriors go through the same form of confession. At the conclusion of this portion of their ceremonies the U-stu-ae-gu-nae, or feather dance, sometimes called the dance of peace, is performed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: The clans are divided for the games - Bear, Deer, Eel and Hawk against Wolf, Beaver, Snipe and Turtle - each holding its feasts in separate houses, even although husband and wife be divided. The gambling then commences and continues three more days, and is considered a religious ceremony. The gambling and betting concluded, two Indians, costumed as medicine men, run into all the houses, and raking up the ashes call on all to repair to the Council House. In the evening of this day begins the 'scaring of witches': speeches are made; Indian songs or chants are sung, while an old man or woman enters, appearing to wish or search for something, the assembly guessing at the object desired.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: On the ensuing day, at a given hour, the white dog is roasted. A perfectly pure, unblemished white dog is selected, and five young men of the most spotless reputation are chosen to kill it; around whose neck two ropes are fastened, and the young men pull the ropes till the dog is strangled. When dead it is presented to the victorious gambling party, who comb out its hair carefully with teasels; it is then decorated with wampum, ribbons, Indian tobacco, strips of buckskin, small baskets, silver brooches. While the fire is being lighted the chiefs chant and praise the Great Spirit, after which, while the warriors are shooting up at the sun, the dog is thrown into the fire, which ceremony unites all the clans. The feast follows, of meats garnished with sunflower oil; the third day of dancing is devoted to the war dance, dedicated to the sun, moon, stars, and thunder.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.

passages.text: At the conclusion of the feather dance the Si-ti-ga-ni-ai, or shuffle dance, follows, executed solely by the women, who do not lift their feet from the floor; then succeeds the guide dance, the closing dance of the new year's festival - after which the medicine men reappear and for a day and a night go about in the houses and chase away all diseases. This closes by all repairing to the Council House, where a large kettle of burnt corn, sweetened with maple sugar, is prepared for the medicine men, who eat it from the kettle; from this Council House fire the medicine men throw the ashes upon the assembled people for the purpose of dispelling witches and disease. This concludes the new year's festival ceremonies after a duration of three weeks.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. VI; public domain.
